finding: §4.2.3.1's whole rule rests on a premise §4.3 contradicts in the same release. §4.2.3.1: "A unit invoked with `--role` holds exactly one prompt, is not the orchestrator, and has no regression prompt to process first" — and from that it strips, under `--role`, every sentence that "direct[s] an action the caller's own payload cannot support", which it enumerates as the spawn-a-sub-agent sentence, the regression-ordering sentence, and the directives to merge, to record the round, and to run the uncounted `--perspective regression` delta pass. But §4.3's P2 paragraph names a second `--role` caller who is exactly the orchestrator: "For a human orchestrator the N case becomes one invocation per role instead of one invocation plus a split script." That caller must merge, must record the round, must run the delta pass, and — per §4.1, where `regression` is 62% of the payload and `--role regression` is explicitly made selectable by §4.2 — must apply the regression findings first. Under §4.2.3.1's rule every one of those directives is removed from every payload that caller receives, on all N invocations, so the interactive path §1 calls this repository's documented fallback loses tp's only statement of how to close a round. The two sections cannot both stand: either `--role` implies non-orchestrator (and §4.3 must retract the human-orchestrator recommendation) or it does not (and §4.2.3.1's predicate cannot be keyed on the flag).
suggestion: Key the filter on something that actually distinguishes the two callers rather than on `--role` alone — the presence of `TP_UNIT_ID`/`TP_ROUND_DIR` is the discriminator the driver already sets and §4.2.3 already relies on for the interactive/driver split — or narrow §4.2.3.1's rule to the sentences that are false for a single-prompt payload regardless of who holds it (the spawn-a-sub-agent and regression-ordering sentences), leaving the merge/record/delta-pass directives intact, and say in §4.3 which form the human orchestrator receives.

finding: This round's rewrite of property 4 defines "recognises" as a union that is not the one §4.2.1 defines, and the two unions disagree on the exit code for a name the spec itself uses as an example — so there is no exit code an implementer can write that satisfies both. Property 4: "'Recognises' is the union of the emitted set, `skipped_roles`, and the corpus for either phase." §4.2.1: exit 2 is for a name "absent from the corpus for either phase, from `skipped_roles`, and from the built-ins." Property 4 has `emitted set` where §4.2.1 has `the built-ins`; neither union contains the other. Measured on the current binary: `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --perspective testing --test-path internal` emits exactly one prompt, role `test-planner`, and its payload's top-level keys are ['perspective','prompts','review_loop','spec','test_path','test_structure'] — no `skipped_roles` key at all. `regression` is refused as a corpus file (§4.1 cites `role id %q is reserved for the built-in regression role`). So for `--perspective testing --role regression`: by §4.2.1 `regression` is a built-in, hence recognised, hence exit 0 with `prompts: []`; by property 4 it is not emitted, not in `skipped_roles` and not in the corpus, hence recognised nowhere, hence exit 2. Property 4's parenthetical claims it is repairing the element "a draft left unnamed", but it names a different third element than §4.2.1 has always carried, so the repair moved the ambiguity rather than closing it.
suggestion: State the recognition set once, in §4.2.1, as a four-element union — the emitted set, `skipped_roles`, the corpus for either phase, and the built-ins — and enumerate the built-ins by name (measured: `regression`, `verifier`, `test-planner`, `documentation-planner`, `code-auditor`). Have property 4 cite §4.2.1's definition instead of restating it, so the two cannot drift again.

finding: The release gate's `tp audit` half emits nothing on a clean working tree, so the gate passes vacuously over exactly half its stated scope at the moment it is meant to run — the release. Property 7 is "for both commands" and property 8 extends it to "every spec in the repository an unrestricted invocation emits prompts for"; §7 makes property 8 the gate and says failing it blocks the release. Measured: `tp audit <spec>` derives its subject from `git diff` on the working tree, and `internal/cli/audit.go:676-681` returns `no changed files detected (staged+unstaged is empty) — use --base <tag> for committed changes, or --affected-files` when that diff is empty. At a release tag, in CI, or in a fresh clone the tree is clean, so the set property 8 quantifies over is EMPTY for `tp audit` and the audit half of the gate is satisfied without emitting a single prompt. When the tree is dirty the half is not vacuous but buys no breadth either: measured across `spec/0.36.0.md`, `spec/0.40.0.md` and `spec/0.42.0.md`, `tp audit` emits the identical four-role panel ['ax-contract','go-safety','maintainability-conventions','spec-coverage'] and the identical 21-entry `files` list for all three — the panel is a function of the working tree, not of the spec. §7's whole breadth argument ("15 with recorded rounds and 7 with none ... the one skip reason that is round-dependent (`regression`, skipped `no-baseline` at round 1 and emitted after)") is a `tp review` state property with no audit analogue, so it justifies breadth only for the half that already has it.
suggestion: Scope property 8 to `tp review` explicitly and give the `tp audit` half its own gate condition with a stated subject that does not depend on uncommitted state — e.g. a fixed `--base <tag>` or an explicit `--affected-files` list pinned by the gate — and say what the audit half is expected to discriminate, since the panel measurably does not vary by spec.

finding: §4.2.3.1 states a rule over `review_loop.instruction` and works it against exactly one of the five mode-specific strings the key actually takes, leaving four unruled — including three where honest application of the rule empties the key entirely, an outcome the section never contemplates. The section quotes only the default-mode string and its entire diagnosis is default-mode-specific ("has no regression prompt to process first"). Measured on the current binary, `review_loop.instruction` is present and different in every legal mode: `--verify` -> 'If verifier finds 0 issues, review is complete. If issues found, run a full review round.'; `--perspective regression` -> 'Spawn a sub-agent with this prompt. Fix what it reports, then generate the next counted round. This pass records no state.'; `--perspective testing` -> 'Spawn a sub-agent with this prompt. Collect the NDJSON plan. Review the plan for completeness, then append the plan to the spec.' Every sentence of the two `--perspective` strings directs an action a single-prompt `--role` caller cannot support (spawn a sub-agent; generate the next counted round; append the plan to the spec — which §2.2's own clause forbids outright), so the rule "no sentence ... may direct an action the caller's own payload cannot support" reduces those keys to the empty string. Property 12's "sentence-subset" permits that, but §4.2.3.1's stated purpose for the first half — "what makes the key honest" — gives an implementer no basis to decide whether an empty instruction is the intended result or a bug. The section's own evidence (`buildReviewLoopInstruction` assembles across nine assignment sites) is offered as the reason not to specify a deletion list, yet the rule replacing it is worked through on one construction out of five.
suggestion: State the rule's scope as all five modes §4.2.2 legalises, quote or cite each mode's current instruction string, and rule explicitly on the empty result: either declare that an instruction with no supportable sentence is emitted as the empty string (or the key omitted), or give the minimum content a `--role` payload must still carry in every mode.

finding: §4.2.3.1's rule rests on a premise about who passes `--role` that §4.3 falsifies, and `--role` carries nothing that lets an implementation tell the two callers apart. §4.2.3.1: "A unit invoked with `--role` holds exactly one prompt, is not the orchestrator, and has no regression prompt to process first." §4.3, selling the same flag: "For a human orchestrator the N case becomes one invocation per role instead of one invocation plus a split script." So the human orchestrator §4.3 targets makes ONLY `--role` invocations, and by §4.2.3.1's rule every one of them is stripped of the sentences that are orchestrator-addressed. Measured, the default-mode key those sentences live in is: 'Merge findings (tp review --merge), verify and resolve them, then record the round: tp review spec/0.36.0.md --record <findings.ndjson>. Repeat until tp review spec/0.36.0.md --status --check exits 0. ... Between counted rounds, you may run tp review spec/0.36.0.md --perspective regression alone as an uncounted delta pass.' Those are the loop-continuation steps only the orchestrator performs, so under §4.3's own recommended usage the operator never sees them in any invocation they make — the release removes the loop's continuation instructions from the only caller who needs them. The rule's antecedent is "the caller's own payload cannot support", but the payload is identical for both callers; what differs is caller identity, which `--role` does not encode. As written the implementer must decide the key's content from information the flag does not carry.
suggestion: Either scope the strip to the driver path only (the driver already sets `TP_UNATTENDED`/`TP_UNIT_ID`, which does distinguish the callers) and leave the interactive `--role` payload's instruction unchanged; or keep the strip unconditional and add to §4.3 what the human orchestrator is expected to read instead, since §4.2.3's brief is the only other instruction surface and it names no merge, record or convergence step.

finding: Properties 1 and 2 were rewritten this round to carry the `output_path` scope §2.3's emission predicate fixes; property 3 was rewritten in the same round without it, and as written properties 2 and 3 contradict each other. Property 3: "An emitted body ends with property 1's suffix, and that same body with its last 468 bytes removed does not also end with it." The subject is "an emitted body", unqualified. Property 2 requires that no prompt whose `output_path` is empty ends with property 1's suffix, and §2.3 states the positive predicate — appended "to every prompt whose `output_path` is non-empty, and to no other". So for the `--perspective` and `--verify` prompts, which property 2 measures and §4.2.2 legalises `--role` in, property 3's first conjunct asserts exactly what property 2 forbids. An implementer writing property 3 literally over every emitted body gets a red test on a correct implementation; one who reads it as scoped is guessing at a scope the neighbouring two properties state explicitly.
suggestion: Give property 3 the same scope its siblings now carry: "Every emitted body whose `output_path` is non-empty ends with property 1's suffix, and that same body with its last 468 bytes removed does not."

finding: Property 2's rewrite this round replaces a written list with a derivation that yields mode NAMES rather than runnable INVOCATIONS, and three of the four names cannot be invoked from anything the spec says. Property 2: "The modes that produce such a prompt are derived from what the code accepts — every `--perspective` value `review.go` validates, plus `--verify` — not from a list written here." Measured just now on a freshly built binary from the repository root, TP_* cleared: `--perspective` validates exactly four values ('must be documentation, testing, code-audit, or regression'), and three of them refuse to emit anything without an extra argument the spec never names — `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --perspective testing` exits 2 with '--test-path is required when --perspective=testing'; `--perspective documentation` exits 2 with '--docs-path is required'; `--perspective code-audit` exits 2 with 'requires at least one --affected-files'. `--docs-path` additionally rejects a file ('--docs-path README.md' exits 3, 'takes a directory that already exists'). So a test author deriving property 2's population as instructed gets five modes and can run two of them (`--perspective regression`, `--verify`) with the information in this spec. Worse, property 2's own supporting measurement is not reproducible from the invocation it names: it states 'Measured on this round's emission, the `--perspective testing` and `--perspective documentation` prompts contain zero occurrences of either', and both of those commands emit no prompt at all — the reader cannot tell which `--test-path`/`--docs-path` produced the quoted result, and §6.1 S2 gives no way to pin them. `code-audit` is a fourth mode the document never mentions anywhere and whose prompt property 2 therefore governs unreviewed.
suggestion: Either name the extra argument each derived mode needs (a directory and an affected-files argument the suite may choose freely, since none of them is review state under S2), or scope property 2's population to the modes the spec has actually measured and say that new `--perspective` values must be added to it deliberately. Re-derive the inline 'zero occurrences' measurement from an invocation that runs, and record the arguments used.

finding: Property 6 classifies by MODE while the only observable is per-INVOCATION, and there are legal modes that emit no prompts — so the release's legality test has two mutually exclusive correct answers. Property 6: "`--role` is accepted in every mode that emits prompts and refused with exit 2 in every mode that emits none, against each command's own flag set (§4.2.2)." §4.2.2 puts `--perspective` wholly in the legal column and makes the ordering load-bearing on the message: "The refusal is evaluated **before** the mode's own argument validation, so the hint an operator sees names the flag conflict rather than a missing `--findings`." Measured on the freshly built binary, repository root, TP_* cleared: `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --perspective code-audit` exits 2 emitting no prompts ('requires at least one --affected-files'); `--perspective testing` and `--perspective documentation` do the same for their own missing arguments; `--verify` without `--findings` likewise ('--verify requires --findings'). So for `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --perspective code-audit --role architect`, engineer A applies property 6 literally — this invocation emits none, therefore refuse with exit 2 and the flag-conflict hint — and engineer B applies §4.2.2's table — `--perspective` is legal, `--role` is never refused there, so the mode's own argument error is what the operator sees. Both exit 2; the hints are opposite; §4.2.2 says the hint is the whole point of the ordering rule. This is not the ordering question round 12 raised about the unrecognised-NAME refusal — that one is about when a name check can run; this one is about which set 'a mode that emits none' denotes, and the spec supplies no membership test for it.
suggestion: State the classifier over the flag set rather than over emission: `--role` is refused in the six/five sub-mode flags §4.2.2's refused column names, and in every other invocation it is accepted and the mode's own argument validation runs normally and reports its own error. Then property 6 asserts a fixed list per command instead of a predicate over a run's output.

finding: §4.2.1 and §6.2.2 property 4 now give two different definitions of "recognises", the single word the exit-0/exit-2 split turns on, and they disagree on names the spec itself names. §4.2.1: a name exits 2 only when "absent from the corpus for either phase, from `skipped_roles`, and from the built-ins" — recognition = corpus(both phases) ∪ skipped_roles ∪ built-ins. Property 4, rewritten this round: "'Recognises' is the union of the emitted set, `skipped_roles`, and the corpus for either phase." The third term differs: property 4 drops the built-ins and substitutes the emitted set. The two sets are not equal and the disagreement is reachable. `tp audit <spec> --role regression`: `regression` is a tp built-in, so §4.2.1 recognises it and requires exit 0 with `prompts: []`; it is in no audit emitted set, in no audit `skipped_roles`, and §4.1 records that `engine.ParseRoleBytes` refuses it as a corpus id, so property 4 recognises it nowhere and requires exit 2. The same split falls out for `verifier`, `test-planner`, `documentation-planner` and `code-auditor` invoked in the default mode — the four names property 4's own parenthetical says "qualify", which they do only under the emitted-set term and only in the mode that emits them. This looks like a round-13 repair applied at one site and not the other: the definition was tightened in §6.2.2 and left as-is in §4.2.1.
suggestion: State the recognition set once, in §4.2.1, and have property 4 cite it rather than restate it. Whichever form is chosen must rule explicitly on `--role regression` under `tp audit` and on a `--verify`/`--perspective` role name passed in the default mode, since those are the names on which the two current forms disagree.

finding: Property 12 has no lower bound, so an empty `review_loop.instruction` — or an absent member — satisfies every property this release states, and this round's edits removed the last text that said otherwise. Property 12: "Under `--role`, `review_loop.instruction` is a sentence-subset of the unrestricted one and contains none of that key's orchestrator-addressed directives." The empty string is a sentence-subset of anything and contains no directive, so `instruction: ""` is green. §4.2.3.1's normative blockquote is the same shape — "no sentence ... may direct an action the caller's own payload cannot support" is vacuously true of zero sentences — and §4.2.3.1 was added this round specifically to WITHDRAW the only positive retention claim the spec ever carried ("A draft said the `--role` form 'keeps the round's convergence statement'. Measured: `convergence` is a sibling key ... so that clause named content the edit does not touch"). Nothing replaced it. Property 4's rule is no help: it exempts the `instruction` member by name, and it does not say whether the member may be absent rather than merely different, so an implementation that deletes the key under `--role` is also unrefuted. Two engineers write opposite assertions from the same text: A asserts the `--role` instruction still carries at least the unit-addressed sentences (where to write, what to produce); B asserts it is empty and cites property 12 as satisfied. Both tests are defensible and they cannot both be green.
suggestion: Add the floor to property 12 in observable terms, e.g. 'Under `--role` the key is present, non-empty, and retains every sentence of the unrestricted instruction that is not orchestrator-addressed' — a subset rule plus a complement rule, which together make the edit exact instead of one-sided. State separately whether the member may be omitted.

finding: §7's premise is a universal over the release's mechanisms and its gate covers one of them, and this round widened the gap without touching §7. §7: "Every mechanism in this release hides, regroups or narrows what a reviewer sees — `--role` most of all — which is the shape that cost v0.34.0 §7.1 eight rounds of suppressed findings. So the release is gated, and the gate is §6.2 property 8." Property 8 is property 7 run over every spec: prompt-set equality under `--role`. It says nothing about the two mechanisms that actually remove content from what a caller reads. §4.2.3.1, added this round, deletes sentences from `review_loop.instruction` and is gated only by property 12, which §6.2.3 itself concedes is "a fixture the task owns: it is a reading, not a computation" — i.e. the new suppression surface is checked by the one property the spec admits is not decidable, and is outside the gate. §2's clause is the second: §2.4 states that it "converts one class of row … from run evidence into asserted evidence, and tp has no verdict for 'asserted, not run'" — a suppression of findings the release creates by its own admission, and no property in §6 measures it. So §7's argument (gate the release because every mechanism suppresses) does not select the gate §7 chooses.
suggestion: Either narrow §7's premise to the mechanism the gate measures — say that property 8 gates `--role`'s panel equality and that §4.2.3.1's and §2's suppression are accepted unmeasured, with the reason — or add the missing gate conditions: for §4.2.3.1, an assertion that the non-`--role` `review_loop.instruction` is unchanged across every spec the gate already iterates (the cheap half of property 12, and decidable); for §2, name it in Non-Goal 2 as deliberately ungated.

finding: §2.3's closing sentence attributes to §6.2 property 3 a figure §1.1 says property 3 does not fix. §2.3: "and no trailing newline. That is 4 separator bytes, which is the figure §1.1 prices and §6.2 property 3 fixes." §1.1 rules the other way, in terms: "§6.2 property 3 fixes the **suffix** at 468 bytes, which is the figure an assertion can reach; 467 is this table's arithmetic on it and no property asserts it separately." Property 3's own text confirms §1.1 — it names 468 and never 4. So the two sections disagree about which number the release's only byte-level property asserts, in text written this round, in the same document whose §1.1 has already recorded four failed attempts to stop exactly this attribution drifting.
suggestion: Drop the second half of the sentence rather than repair it — §1.1 is the derivation and §2.3 is the construction, and neither needs to state what the other's property asserts. "and no trailing newline; the two separator pairs are the 4 bytes §1.1's table prices."

finding: §4.2.3 prices the driver-path redundancy of `--role` at "one redundant token under `tp run`", and §4.2.1 contradicts that price in this release's own text: "This split is forced by the driver, not chosen for taste. §4.2.3's brief change makes `--role <id>` a *unit's own first command*, and the unit set and the emitted set are computed by different filters." So what admitting the flag into the driver's brief actually buys on that path is the whole exit-0/exit-2 recognition apparatus: the five-reason skip table, the three-element definition of "recognises" (§6.2 property 4), the "A unit that receives no prompt still creates its findings file, empty" instruction, and property 5 with fixtures for the four skip reasons §7 says this repository cannot produce. In a release whose §1.1 prices a 468-byte suffix to the byte and defends the −1, the single sentence pricing this release's only change outside the emitter understates it by an entire subsection — and it is the sentence a reader checking whether the flag pays for itself will land on.
suggestion: Replace "at the cost of one redundant token under `tp run`" with the cost §4.2.1 already attributes to this decision, and state the trade rather than hiding it: the flag exists for the interactive path, and putting it in the driver's brief is what forces §4.2.1's recognition rule and property 5's fixtures. If that price is not worth paying, name the alternative it displaces — the driver not spawning a unit whose role emits no prompt, which removes the unit-set/emitted-set divergence at its source instead of specifying an exit code for it.

finding: §4.2.3's second paragraph pins implementation mechanism the spec cannot settle: it names `UnitKind.BriefCommand` as the wrong seam, states that it takes a `UnitTarget`, that `roleUnits` passes the role id as a separate argument to `newNextUnit`, and then concludes only that "The change belongs where both are known" without naming a function. Every clause of it can be established only against code, and its durable output is a negative constraint on a call graph rather than a requirement — the canonical over-specification shape, prescribed here where a task's acceptance settles it by compiling. It is also the second version of this paragraph: the first named a seam that round 13 measured wrong, and the repair added bytes instead of removing the claim. The cost is panel-multiplied — tp embeds changed spec sections verbatim, so this paragraph is re-read by every role in the panel §4 exists to shrink, and it goes stale the next time the call graph moves.
suggestion: Cut the paragraph to the requirement — 'the brief a role unit receives carries `--role <unit id>`; the id must be in scope wherever that brief is built' — and let the implementing task's acceptance name the function and prove it by compiling. §6's preamble already draws exactly this line for tests ('choosing the fixtures, the harness and the assertions is a task's acceptance'); §4.2.3 is the same altitude error on a production seam.

finding: §4.2.3.1 makes `review_loop.instruction` a normative subject of this release and §6.2 property 12 governs its `--role` form, but neither looks at what the key already spends. Measured on the current binary's round-14 emission for this spec: the key is 733 bytes, of which the absolute spec path occurs four times at 61 bytes each — 244 bytes, 33.3% — while `spec_path` is a sibling top-level key on the same payload already carrying that string once, and §6.2 property 4 pins it as unchanged under the flag. Property 12's rule ("a sentence-subset of the unrestricted one") preserves every one of those four repetitions under `--role`, so the release's own byte-reduction mechanism ships a key that is a third redundant with the key beside it. 244 bytes is over half the 468-byte suffix §1.1 spends a table and three paragraphs pricing, which is the accounting asymmetry: this spec measures the bytes it adds to the byte and does not measure the bytes it is already emitting in the one key it just took ownership of.
suggestion: Either state that the key's *content* is out of scope and price it, so the asymmetry with §1.1 is a visible decision rather than an omission; or add one sentence to §4.2.3.1 — under `--role`, surviving sentences refer to the spec through the `spec_path` key rather than repeating the absolute path. The second adds no surface and removes 183 bytes per invocation, the same order as the 467 §1.1 adds per prompt.

finding: §4.2.3.1's closing paragraph declines to correct a sentence it concedes is false on the principle "this release's scope is what a `--role` caller receives". The release falsifies that principle two sections earlier: §2 and §3 append 468 bytes to *every* prompt on every path, `--role` or not, and §1.1 exists to price exactly that change to what every non-`--role` caller reads. So the stated reason for the deferral is not a rule this release follows. What is deferred is measured and live — confirmed on the current binary's round-14 emission for this spec, which emits four role prompts plus `regression` while `review_loop.instruction` still says "before or together with the three role prompts" — so every unrestricted caller receives a miscount of its own panel every round. Unlike §3.1 and Non-Goal 6, which state their open questions and refuse to invent an owner, this deferral names neither an owner nor a release.
suggestion: Either make the correction — it is a wording change to one sentence, with no new surface, no knob and no test to write — or drop the scope claim and record the deferral the way §3.1 does: state that no spec owns it, so it is visibly open rather than closed-looking. Do not rest it on a scope principle §2 and §3 break.

finding: Non-Goal 7 enumerates this release's exceptions to "nothing changes" and is now short by one. It reads: "Changing what a round asks. The checklist items, role rules and output schema are untouched. The prompt does gain two behavioural clauses — that is §2 and §3, and §1 prices them; the claim here is narrower than 'nothing changes'." §4.2.3.1, added this round, changes a third thing a caller receives — `review_loop.instruction`, a key §4.2.3.1 itself calls "a shipped contract" and "emitted on every review payload". §1's overview omits it too, listing only the prompt clauses, `--role` and the brief change ("the release's only change outside the emitter"). A prior round produced the identical finding against §1 for the brief change and it was repaired at §1 alone; the same enumeration defect now exists for the instruction change at both sites. This matters beyond bookkeeping because §4.2.3.1 rests part of its own argument on what Non-Goal 7 does and does not say ("not a prohibition read into Non-Goal 7, which speaks about checklist items, role rules and the output schema and says nothing about this key"), so a reader checking that claim against an enumeration that omits the change has nothing to check it with.
suggestion: Add the instruction change to both enumerations: in §1, alongside the brief change; in Non-Goal 7, as a third named exception — "and the `--role` form of `review_loop.instruction` (§4.2.3.1)" — so the Non-Goal states what it excludes rather than being cited as evidence that the change was never in scope.

finding:
After this round's rewrite of §6.2.1, no property in the release can fail on an implementation that omits the trailing-newline strip — the one byte §1.1 calls 'not optional and not cosmetic'. Property 1 names the strip inside a CONSTRUCTION ('trailing newline removed, then `LF LF`, §2.2's clause, `LF LF`, §3.2's clause, no trailing newline') but quantifies only over the emitted artifact ('Every emitted prompt ... ends with'). Work it through: §1.1 measures that every role prompt body already ends with `
`, so a non-stripping implementation emits `...body
` + `

` + c1 + `

` + c2. That string ends with `

`+c1+`

`+c2, so the natural HasSuffix assertion from property 1 is GREEN. Property 3 is equally blind: remove the last 468 bytes and the remainder is `...body
`, which does not end with the suffix, so property 3 is GREEN too. Property 2 governs a disjoint population. And §1.1 closes the last exit itself: '§6.2 property 3 fixes the **suffix** at 468 bytes, which is the figure an assertion can reach; 467 is this table's arithmetic on it and no property asserts it separately' — the net delta is exactly the figure that would have caught the missing strip. Verified arithmetically against the spec's own strings: §2.2's clause is 287 bytes and §3.2's is 177, so suffix 468 / net 467 are both correct; it is the assertion coverage, not the arithmetic, that is missing. Two engineers write different tests — one asserts only the suffix, one additionally asserts the byte at offset -469 is not LF — and only the second can fail on the defect §1.1 exists to prevent.
suggestion: Make the strip a property of the artifact rather than a step of the construction: add to property 1 that the byte immediately preceding the suffix is not `LF` (equivalently, that the emitted body contains no three-LF run at the join). That is decidable on one live emission with no fixture and no second version, which is the standard §6.2.1 already sets for itself.

finding: Property 11 is the only property in §6.2 that names no command, and the command it silently omits is the one where it cannot be evaluated. Every sibling scopes itself: property 1 'Holds for `tp review` and `tp audit`', property 6 'against each command's own flag set', property 7 'for both commands', property 10 keys off §4.2.1's table which is explicitly a union across both. Property 11 reads only: 'The emitted role set minus the unit set is exactly `{regression}` at a round where `regression` emits, as set equality.' `regression` is a `tp review` built-in — §4.1 derives it from `buildReviewPrompts` and §6.2 property 5 says so outright ('`no-baseline` is `tp review`'s built-in regression role'). Measured on the freshly built binary: `tp audit spec/0.36.0.md` emits exactly the four corpus roles (ax-contract, go-safety, maintainability-conventions, spec-coverage), the same four that are units, so the difference is the empty set, not `{regression}`. An engineer therefore cannot tell which of three tests to write for the audit half: the property is review-only (no assertion), it is vacuous for audit because no audit round satisfies its 'at a round where `regression` emits' precondition (no assertion, but for a different and unstated reason), or it applies and audit's empty difference makes it red. §4.4 compounds it by stating the defect the property pins in review-only terms ('The regression prompt reaching four units and no unit') while §4.2 applies `--role` to both commands.
suggestion: Scope property 11 explicitly, as its siblings do: state that it is a `tp review` property and that `tp audit`'s emitted role set equals its unit set with no exception — which is itself a set equality worth pinning, since it is the invariant that would break if audit ever gained a built-in role.
